a:r.a:t: R13 STAGE SCRIPT | SLIDE 08 |
The control system
Design the control architecture while framing the project. A diagram cannot guarantee reliability. We need evidence that the controls work.
Enforce sensitive data access and account permissions outside the model. Check text output too: a disclosure needs no tool call.
The loop needs evidence, interpretation, decision authority and timely action. Then verify that the intervention worked.

Include models, monitoring, human review and recovery in the cost. If the whole system is not viable, reduce scope or fund more R&D. Complex cases may need a control engineer or mathematician. Sometimes we should not proceed.

Where automation is insufficient, a trained human may be the best available control. Their skills, workload, information and authority become architectural dependencies. This is a socio-technical system.

For DevOps and SRE, monitor that human control at runtime. Beyond availability, track qualified coverage, queues, workload and response time. Check whether people have the information and authority to act, and whether interventions work. Fatigue is harder to measure directly; workload can signal strain.
If capacity falls, reduce autonomy, use a tested fallback or pause.
An operator can be online while their control is already failing.

For teams building their first agentic applications, a successful demo alone does not justify funding full development. We also need to understand the control architecture. This can reveal a different risk landscape, identify missing expertise and improve the budget forecast. The project's direction can change before the development budget is committed.
==== REFERENCE NOTES AND SOURCES (NOT STAGE SCRIPT) ====

The engineered object is the entire consequential path, not only the model: proposals are untrusted, semantic checks are fallible, and sensitive effects require independently enforced policy and permission boundaries.
For account recovery, the assistant may guide a verified-address recovery but must not redirect credentials to a new unverified destination; rejected or unavailable paths fall back safely.
DevOps and SRE must observe real outcomes and control health, know who can stop or narrow authority, and verify that rerouting, manual fallback or another correction actually worked in time.

For novel consequential systems, do not commit to a typical implementation budget before testing feasibility and funding domain experts, evaluations, technical gates, staffed operations and a contingency for redesign or stopping.
This is the operational evidence needed for the distinct business and architectural conclusions on the final slide.
Expanded talk track / source qualifications:

The route is a simplified teaching architecture, not a validated universal blueprint. Model proposal and retrieved text are untrusted. A second LLM checking an answer is fallible and may share assumptions with the generator; independently grounded business-policy examples and forbidden-case tests are needed to evaluate meaning. The example lets an assistant send a recovery link to a previously verified address and prohibits changing a destination to a new unverified address without independent identity proof. A deterministic tool gate enforces user-data rights and approval on the complete authorized execution path, but the advice/answer path still needs relevant semantic and data-loss controls; read-only does not imply consequence-free. Controls must be measured for false allows, false denials, bypass, failure mode and recovery, not just logged as present. Feedback after an irreversible privacy leak cannot repair that leak; impose preventive permission control. Incident owner and service owner must have rights, knowledge, on-call time and available staffing; Product/BA/domain set the unacceptable results, QA and Dev produce meaningful evidence, Architect/SRE build enforceable boundaries, release/risk owner accepts scope, and delivery leadership funds the dependencies. These are duties, not mandated new job titles. Before project commitment, compare current workflow and simplest safe alternative with the AI path under matched outcomes, risks and full operating cost. For genuinely novel consequential agentic products, first fund a bounded feasibility stage: domain expertise, adverse-case evaluation, enforceable boundary verification, safe behavior monitoring and on-call capacity. A discovery result may be to narrow scope, remove autonomy, choose a deterministic alternative or stop; unknown feasibility should not be sold as a guaranteed fixed-scope delivery estimate. DevOps/SRE need actionable behavior/control signals, an explicit stop authority and tested manual fallback, with an incident owner who can verify the correction actually changed outcomes. Scope can be broad, bounded, changed or no AI. Transition to S09: this control loop is the engineering test for whether consequential delegation is operationally viable, with human response capacity and full cost, not the final thesis itself. The final slide alone synthesizes HOW WE BUILD and WHAT WE BUILD into two research directions. Target 3:00, rehearse.

ns2:r.ns2:t: Treat this loop as a hypothesis to test for the particular use case. Sensors must detect relevant outcomes and control failures, and a human may contribute contextual observation or interpretation. The controller compares evidence with goals and limits and may rely on a human decision and authority. When either level relies on people, their availability, competence, workload, response time and authority become architectural dependencies that operations must observe. Constraints bound what actuators can do before consequences. Feedback must show whether the correction worked.

ns3:r.ns3:t: A successful happy-path demo is useful evidence of capability, but it does not establish that the proposed control loop is adequate or economical. Before committing full development, test detection, prevention or limitation of harm, and timely intervention against the business context, acceptable risk and full cost, including models, controls, staffed operations and recovery. If evidence is insufficient, fund bounded discovery. If control or cost is inadequate, narrow scope, redesign or decide no-go. The scope and decision depend on the use case.
